text: Every data flow's monitoring view breaks execution down into four genuinely possible bottlenecks. Cluster start-up time, spinning up the Spark cluster itself, usually three to five minutes. Reading from a source. Transformation time, at whichever stage actually takes the longest. And writing to a sink. Find the largest number first — that's where tuning effort genuinely pays off, not wherever intuition happens to point.

Every transformation carries an Optimize tab, controlling how data actually gets repartitioned across the Spark cluster after that specific step. Use current partitioning is the default, and genuinely the right choice in most real scenarios — repartitioning itself takes real time, so only override it deliberately.

When you do need to override it, five real strategies exist. Round robin when no good key candidates exist at all. Hash when you want similar values grouped together, though test for skew first. And Key partitioning for genuinely high-cardinality data, one partition per unique value. Single partition, combining everything into one, is strongly discouraged outside a specific business reason — it's slow, and it drags down every downstream step too.

By default, data flows log Verbose telemetry — full detail at every individual partition, which is genuinely expensive to produce. Basic logs only transformation durations. None gives just a summary. Reserve Verbose specifically for when you're actively troubleshooting something — running it by default on every production run is a real, entirely avoidable performance cost.

Find the bottleneck first, then tune deliberately — that's the whole discipline this lesson teaches. Chapter 5 is complete. Next, Chapter 6: triggers and scheduling — everything you've built across this entire course so far, finally running entirely on its own.
